A: Chapter 13 (35 verses in this edition; 34 in the 700-verse vulgate, which lacks 13.1) distinguishes the field (kṣetra) from its knower (kṣetrajña). Movements: 13.1 Arjuna asks about prakṛti and puruṣa, the field and its knower, knowledge and the knowable. 13.2–5 Kṛṣṇa calls the body the field and the one who knows it the knower of the field, declares himself the knower in all fields, calls the knowledge of both 'knowledge', and says this has been sung by the seers, in the metres and in the brahmasūtra words. 13.6–7 the field listed with its modifications (the great elements, ahaṅkāra, buddhi, the unmanifest, the senses and their ranges, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience, steadiness). 13.8–12 twenty dispositions, from absence of pride to keeping in view the aim of knowledge of reality, are declared 'knowledge'; what differs from them is ignorance. 13.13–19 the knowable: brahman, beginningless and supreme, called neither being nor non-being, with hands, feet and eyes everywhere, without guṇas yet experiencing them, inside and outside beings, undivided yet as if divided, light of lights, set in the heart of all; knowing this the devotee becomes fit for Kṛṣṇa's state. 13.20–24 prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless; prakṛti is the cause in agency, puruṣa in experiencing; attachment to the guṇas causes births; the highest puruṣa in the body is named onlooker, consenter, supporter, experiencer, great lord and supreme self; one who knows this is not born again. 13.25–26 some see the self by meditation, others by sāṃkhya-yoga, others by karma-yoga; others worship on hearing from others and they too cross death. 13.27–35 every being is born from the union of field and knower; one who sees the supreme lord the same in all beings, prakṛti as doer and the self as non-doer, and the many resting in the one, truly sees and attains brahman; the supreme self, beginningless and without guṇas, neither acts nor is tainted, like space, and illumines the field as the sun the world; those who know the difference of field and knower with the eye of knowledge go to the supreme. The purpose the chapter states: knowledge of the field and its knower and of their difference (13.3, 13.35).
B: Chapter 13 (in this edition 35 verses; 34 in the 700-verse numbering) distinguishes the field (kṣetra) from its knower (kṣetrajña). Movements: Arjuna asks about prakṛti and puruṣa, field and knower, knowledge and the knowable (13.1, only in editions with the extra verse). The body is the field and whoever knows it is its knower; the Lord is the knower in all fields, and knowing field and knower is knowledge (13.2-13.3). The subject is announced as sung by the seers and in the brahma-sūtra words (13.4-13.5). The field is enumerated: elements, the sense of 'I', understanding, the unmanifest, the faculties and their objects, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain and others (13.6-13.7). Twenty dispositions, from absence of pride to seeing the aim of the knowledge of reality, are called knowledge; the rest is ignorance (13.8-13.12). The knowable is the beginningless highest brahman, neither being nor non-being, described by paradox as everywhere and nowhere confined, the light of lights seated in the heart (13.13-13.18); the Lord's devotee who understands this comes to his state (13.19). Prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless; prakṛti is the cause of agency, puruṣa of experiencing; attachment to the guṇas causes births; the highest person in the body is onlooker, sustainer and supreme self; whoever knows this is not born again (13.20-13.24). People see the self by meditation, by sāṃkhya, by the yoga of action, or worship after hearing from others (13.25-13.26). Every being arises from the union of field and knower; the one who sees the Lord equally in all, sees prakṛti as the doer and oneself as not the doer, and sees the manifold as resting in the one, sees truly and reaches brahman (13.27-13.31). The beginningless supreme self does not act and is not stained, like space; it illumines the field as the sun the world (13.32-13.34). Those who know the difference of field and knower with the eye of knowledge go to the highest (13.35).

A: Chapter 14 (27 verses) sets out the three guṇas. Movements: 14.1–2 Kṛṣṇa announces again the highest knowledge, by which the sages reached the highest perfection and came to share his nature, not born at creation nor troubled at dissolution. 14.3–4 the great brahman is his womb; he places the embryo in it and is the seed-giving father of all forms. 14.5–10 sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the embodied one — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by heedlessness, idleness and sleep — and each prevails by overpowering the other two. 14.11–13 the signs of each when increased. 14.14–15 where one goes on dying in each. 14.16–18 their fruits and their upward, middle and downward courses. 14.19–20 one who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains Kṛṣṇa's state, and going beyond the three guṇas attains the immortal, freed from birth, death, old age and pain. 14.21 Arjuna asks the marks, the conduct and the means of one gone beyond the guṇas. 14.22–25 the marks and conduct: not hating or longing for the guṇas' effects, unshaken, knowing 'the guṇas operate', the same in pleasure and pain, praise and blame, honour and dishonour, friend and foe, relinquishing all undertakings. 14.26–27 the means: serving Kṛṣṇa with unswerving devotion one goes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for becoming brahman — for he is the foundation of brahman, of the immortal, of everlasting dharma and of absolute happiness. The purpose the chapter states: knowledge of how the guṇas bind and of the way beyond them (14.1–2, 14.19–26).
B: Chapter 14 (27 verses) sets out the three guṇas and the way beyond them. Movements: the Lord announces again the highest knowledge, by which sages reached perfection and are not reborn at creation nor troubled at dissolution (14.1-14.2). Great brahman is his womb, in which he places the germ; he is the seed-giving father of all forms (14.3-14.4). Sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the embodied one: sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by heedlessness, indolence and sleep (14.5-14.9). Each prevails by overpowering the others, and each has its signs: light and knowledge; greed, activity and restlessness; darkness, inactivity, heedlessness and delusion (14.10-14.13). The guṇa that prevails at death decides the next birth, and each has its fruit and direction — upward, middle, downward (14.14-14.18). The seer who sees no doer but the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains the Lord's state; going beyond the guṇas one attains immortality (14.19-14.20). Arjuna asks for the marks, conduct and means of the one beyond the guṇas (14.21); the Lord describes his evenness and non-involvement (14.22-14.25) and names the means: unswerving devotion, which makes one fit for becoming brahman (14.26). The Lord is the foundation of brahman, the immortal, everlasting dharma and absolute happiness (14.27).
resolution: merged: Chapter 14 (27 verses) sets out the three guṇas and the way beyond them. A: Chapter 15 (20 verses) moves from the world-tree to the highest person. Movements: 15.1–2 the imperishable aśvattha with roots above and branches below, its leaves the metres, its branches swollen by the guṇas with the sense-objects as shoots, its roots below bound up with action in the human world; to know it is to know the Veda. 15.3–6 its form, end, beginning and foundation are not perceived here; it is to be cut with the weapon of non-attachment and the place of no return sought, with the words 'I take refuge in that primal person'; those free of pride, delusion, attachment and desire, intent on the self and released from the pairs reach that imperishable place, unlit by sun, moon or fire, Kṛṣṇa's supreme abode. 15.7–11 an eternal portion of Kṛṣṇa, become the living being, draws the senses and mind, carries them from body to body as wind carries scents, and enjoys objects through them; the deluded do not see it, those with the eye of knowledge and striving yogins do. 15.12–15 Kṛṣṇa is the radiance in sun, moon and fire, sustains beings, nourishes plants as Soma, digests food as Vaiśvānara, is seated in the heart of all, the source of memory, knowledge and their loss, the one to be known by all the Vedas, maker of the vedānta and knower of the Veda. 15.16–20 there are two persons in the world, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the one standing firm), and the highest person, another, called the supreme self, the imperishable lord; Kṛṣṇa, beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable, is the puruṣottama; one who knows him so knows all and worships him with his whole being; this is the most secret teaching, understanding which one is wise and has done what is to be done. The purpose the chapter states: to make known the puruṣottama (15.18–20).
B: Chapter 15 (20 verses) is the teaching of the highest person (puruṣottama). Movements: the imperishable aśvattha with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic metres, its branches nourished by the guṇas and its roots binding through action in the human world (15.1-15.2); it is to be cut with the weapon of non-attachment, and the place of no return sought, taking refuge in the primal person (15.3-15.4); those free of pride, delusion, attachment, desire and the pairs reach it; it is the Lord's supreme abode, not lit by sun, moon or fire (15.5-15.6). An eternal portion of the Lord, become the living being, draws the senses and mind, carries them from body to body and enjoys objects; the deluded do not see it, those with the eye of knowledge and striving yogins do (15.7-15.11). The Lord is the radiance of sun, moon and fire, sustains beings by entering the earth, nourishes plants as soma, digests food as vaiśvānara, is seated in the heart of all and is what all the Vedas make known (15.12-15.15). There are two persons, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable; the highest person, the supreme self, is another, and the Lord, being beyond both, is called puruṣottama (15.16-15.18). Whoever knows him thus worships him with all his being (15.19). This most secret teaching makes one wise and one who has done what is to be done (15.20).
